MENA Policy Observatory

This observatory gathers official sources and public policy on digital accessibility, shows what each document says, where it says it, and what has not yet been verified. The aim is comparison that can be checked, not a compliance verdict.

What this observatory is

The observatory is a bilingual research catalogue of public policies that affect digital accessibility in the Middle East and North Africa. For each document it records the reported official source, the scope, a research summary, and the interpretation questions that remain open. It does not provide legal advice and it does not issue compliance certificates.

Why use it

Use it to find official sources, compare how governments describe accessibility duties, and see what is still unresolved. Every record keeps the source text, the research summary, and the interpretation alternatives separate.

  • Direct links to the reported official sources.
  • A visible legal-review state for every record, never an assumed one.
  • Open questions shown explicitly instead of being hidden behind a final answer.

Current pilot

This release publishes 11 research records covering 6 of 24 listed jurisdictions: the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar. Digital accessibility is the only researched policy area. Every other listed country is marked as not yet researched, and no other policy area has records yet.

What “Rules as Code” means

Rules as Code means converting written rules into structured, machine-readable logic that a computer can apply to a described case. It is an encoding method, not a new source of legal authority. A program can apply the text it was given; it cannot decide what the text means.

Axiom is the rule engine this project is evaluating. A RuleSpec is a candidate machine-readable representation of one provision. In this release every RuleSpec is an empty scaffold: there are no rules to compile or run, and no engine version is pinned.

No candidate rule in this release is certified, legally approved, or independently reviewed. A rule may only be described that way when the source, interpretation, tests, and review evidence are recorded.

How a claim becomes a candidate rule

Each stage is separate evidence. A later stage does not upgrade an earlier one.

  1. Source Locate the official instrument and record its URL, the language of the copy consulted, and when it was captured.
  2. Clause Point to the exact section, page, or paragraph. Without a locator, a claim stays unverified.
  3. Interpretation Record what the clause could mean, the alternatives, and the questions that remain open.
  4. Candidate rule Encode one interpretation as a RuleSpec, with its assumptions and limits written down.
  5. Test Run positive, negative, boundary, and indeterminate cases against a pinned engine version.
  6. Independent review A qualified reviewer checks the source, the interpretation, and the test evidence. The build itself cannot approve a rule.

Why missing evidence is not “no law”

An empty cell, a missing record, or an open question means the research has not established an answer. It does not mean that no law exists, that a duty does not apply, or that a country has no policy. This site records that difference explicitly instead of turning uncertainty into a “no”.

What this release does not claim

  • No compliance certification for any organisation or website.
  • No country ranking or comparison score.
  • No draft policy treated as law in force.
  • No link presented as proof of legal effect.
  • No machine-executable rule described as legally approved.

Research status in this release

  • 11 research records are published, all on digital accessibility.
  • 6 of 24 listed jurisdictions have at least one record.
  • 0 of 11 records have an encoded rule; every RuleSpec file is an empty scaffold.
  • 0 of 11 records have a confirmed legal-effect finding.
  • Arabic and French page text is a draft pending native review. Policy record fields are shown in their source language with language marking.
